questions.q: What does Second Normal Form (2NF) require?
options: Every non-key column must depend on the entire composite primary key, not just part of it
Every table must have at least two columns
Every column must be nullable
Every table must have a foreign key
questions.explain: 2NF only applies where there's a composite key, and it forbids a column depending on just part of that key.

options: A non-key column that depends on only part of a composite key, instead of the whole key
A foreign key that references only part of another table's primary key
A column that is sometimes NULL
An index that covers only some of a table's rows
questions.explain: This is the specific violation 2NF is designed to eliminate.

questions.q: How does AdventureWorks2012's Sales.SalesOrderDetail avoid a 2NF violation?
options: It stores only ProductID, not ProductName, even though its composite key includes SalesOrderDetailID — the name is fetched via a join to Production.Product
It stores ProductName directly on every row for fast reads
It has no primary key at all
It duplicates ProductName across every order for the same product
questions.explain: ProductName depends only on ProductID, not the whole composite key, so storing it directly would violate 2NF — SalesOrderDetail avoids this by not storing it.

questions.q: What does Third Normal Form (3NF) forbid that 2NF doesn't already cover?
options: A transitive dependency — a non-key column depending on another non-key column instead of directly on the primary key
Any table having more than one foreign key
Storing dates in a DATE column
Using composite primary keys at all
questions.explain: 3NF goes further than 2NF by also disallowing non-key-to-non-key dependencies.

questions.q: What is the simple test for checking any of the normal forms?
options: Ask whether each column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key
Count the number of rows in the table
Check whether the table has an index
Check whether the table name starts with 'dbo.'
questions.explain: This mnemonic maps directly to 1NF (atomic), 2NF (whole key), and 3NF (nothing but the key).
